title: Regional orchestration and routing scopes (ownership sketch)
content:
Purpose:
Quick, pragmatic proposal + ownership sketch for how the control plane should partition responsibilities across: API gateway surface, orchestration layer (routing + policy), and runtime adapters (model runtime, quantization, hardware selection). Focus is multi-region behaviour: failover, locality, cost-aware routing and service ownership boundaries that map to teams.

Context / Motivation:
- We are operating in 3+ regions and will add private deployments. Current routing logic is embedded in gateway and a mix of ad-hoc fallbacks in runtime adapters. Hard to reason about ownership and debugging (who owns a cross-region routing decision?).
- Goal: make routing decisions explicit, auditable, and owned. Separation of concerns: 
  * Gateway = ingress, auth, request normalization, initial policy evaluation (fast, cached).
  * Orchestration = policy engine, routing decisions, rollouts, canary rules, multi-region failover orchestration.
  * Runtime adapters = translate routing -> concrete runtime actions (select model variant, node pool, quantization profile), expose capacity signals.

High-level decision: route-by-policy, not by hard-coded region precedence. The orchestration layer evaluates a policy language and emits a ranked set of endpoint targets with metadata (region, cost_est, expected_latency_ms). Gateway consumes the top-ranked target and attaches routing headers for adapters.

Routing policy primitives (proposal):
- prefer_region: [us-west, eu-central] (ordered preference)
- latency_limit_ms: 80
- cost_budget_per_token_cents: 0.025
- isolation: {private: true | false} (tenant isolation requirement)
- compliance_tags: [pci,hipaa] (must-route-only-to set of allowed deployment types)
- capacity_threshold_pct: 20 (do not route to targets with < threshold available)

Example policy (text form):
- policy-id: low-latency-us
  prefer_region: [us-west,us-east]
  latency_limit_ms: 50
  cost_budget_per_token_cents: 0.05

Decision flow (sequence):
1) Client -> API gateway (auth, quota check, quick cache lookup for recent routing decisions)
2) Gateway asks Orchestration: "route(request-context, policy-hints)" (lightweight call)
3) Orchestration evaluates policy graph (see below) and returns ranked endpoints + route-id
4) Gateway forwards request to chosen endpoint with route-id and advisory headers (x-rd-route-id, x-rd-fallback-list)
5) Runtime adapter receives request, validates headers, attempts local dispatch. On rejection (capacity/health) adapter returns structured failure and optional suggested fallback index -> Gateway/Orchestration reconciles and retries using next target

Ownership map (sketch):
- API Gateway team (eng-console-and-tooling):
  * owns ingress surface, auth, request normalization, per-tenant quotas, header conventions, short-term cache for route decisions (TTL ~5s)
  * owns retry semantics and immediate adapter failure handling (transparent retries for adapter-level transient failures)
- Orchestration team (eng-platform-engineering core):
  * owns policy language, evaluation engines, multi-region inventory, decision logging, route-id generation, rollouts/canaries, and the orchestration API used by gateway.
  * exposes "policy simulator" and timeline-based rollouts for product teams to test routing effects.
- Runtime Adapters (serving-runtime + infra owning teams):
  * own adapter contracts, capacity reporting API, health checks, version compatibility for model variants, and region-local optimizations (kernel choices, quantization presets).
  * small shim per runtime type (tpu/gpu/cpu) maintained by respective infra subteams.

Concrete interfaces (lightweight):
- Orchestration -> Inventory DB: get capacity/cost/latency estimates (owned by infra-metrics)
- Gateway -> Orchestration: POST /route/evaluate {request-context, policy-hints} -> returns {route_id, targets:[{id, region, endpoint, est_latency_ms, cost_per_token}]}
- Gateway -> Adapter: HTTP gRPC call with route-id and advisory header. Adapter must implement quick capacity check endpoint and explicit 409/503 responses with structured reason codes.

Multi-region failover rules (proposal):
- Soft-failover: Orchestration returns primary targets but gateway holds fallback list for fast retry without re-evaluating policy for 1s. Useful for transient per-adapter rejections.
- Hard-failover: After two gateway-level retries within 5s OR detection of region-wide outage (via health feed), gateway must call orchestration for a re-eval to prefer alternate regions and update route-id.
- Geo-stickiness: optional per-tenant flag. If enabled, orchestration pins preferred-region for session length up to N minutes unless performance/capacity issues degrade.

Observability and debugging needs (ownership implications):
- Orchestration must log decision traces and store route_id -> decision tree. This is the source-of-truth for "why traffic went to X". (Owning team: eng-platform-engineering).
- Gateway must emit route_id in request logs and tracing spans (Owning team: gateway team).
- Adapters must annotate spans with chosen node, HW type, model-variant and returned cost tokens. Also emit capacity heartbeat metrics.

Rollout and migration plan (3 phases):
- Phase 0 (experiments): feature-flag orchestration endpoint; gateway still uses existing fallback logic but writes decision traces for telemetry. Duration: 3 weeks. Owner: orchestrations + gateway.
- Phase 1 (soft-switch): gateway queries orchestration but will only use orchestration decision if confidence_score>0.7. Keep adapter shim compatibility mode. Duration: 4 weeks.
- Phase 2 (hard-switch): full orchestration-driven routing with deprecation of old heuristic. Provide rollback flag at orchestration. Duration: 2 weeks + monitoring ramp.

Open questions / tradeoffs (bulleted):
- Where to keep TTL for cached route decisions? Short TTL reduces stale routing but increases load on orchestration. Proposal: split TTL by request class: interactive shorts=2s, bulk=30s.
- Policy evaluation latency SLO: target < 10ms p95. If we cannot reach this, move lightweight policies into gateway and reserve orchestration for complex policies.
- How strict should adapters be about rejecting requests for capacity reasons? Over-eager rejection increases cross-service chatter. Proposal: adapters expose a graded rejection: soft_reject (suggested fallback) vs hard_reject.
- How to handle private deployments where orchestration control plane is customer-managed? We need a 'local-only' mode in the policy language and a mechanism to trust local inventory signals.

Minimal adapter contract (text summary for engineers):
- /v1/health: returns {status, capacity_percent, supported_models:list}
- /v1/check_capacity?route_id=XYZ : returns {ok:true|false, reason_code, suggested_fallback_index}
- request payload must accept route_id header and correlate in logs

Example trace (ascii):
Client -> Gateway (route request) -> Orchestration [evaluates policy] -> Gateway -> Adapter A (capacity check ok) -> Adapter A executes -> returns. If A soft_rejects -> Gateway tries Adapter B from fallback list without full re-eval (soft-failover). If B hard_rejects -> Gateway calls Orchestration for re-eval (hard-failover).

Ownership notes / who to call:
- If routing decisions are nondeterministic or trace missing -> contact eng-platform-engineering (orchestration)
- If header conventions, auth, or quota mismatch -> contact API Gateway team
- If adapter health/capacity mismatch -> contact serving-runtime infra owners

Next steps / immediate action items:
- eng-platform-engineering: draft minimal evaluation API and proto. (owner: Priya)
- gateway: add route-id propagation and short-lived cache hook (owner: Miguel)
- runtime adapters: implement /v1/check_capacity shim and structured failure codes (owner: Zoe)
- infra-metrics: define inventory telemetry schema and cost model export (owner: Liam)
- Schedule 1-week health check after Phase 0 to review traces and tune policy defaults.

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep policy language small at first; avoid full-blown DSL until we have 2 months of telemetry.
- Favor explicitness: route_id is critical for debugging across teams.
- Customers on private deployments: add "local_only" flag in policy so orchestration doesn't advertise cross-region targets.

Unresolved: exact JSON schema for orchestration response and adapter failure codes. Will draft separate tiny PR with examples.

End of sketch.
